title: REG U4·W2 — Nontaxable Exchanges & Special Dispositions (2026)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — deferring the tax on a disposition

Not every gain is taxed when realized. The Code lets taxpayers defer gain on certain exchanges and dispositions — the §1031 like-kind exchange MBG uses to roll one parcel into another, the §1033 deferral when property is condemned, the §121 exclusion on a home sale, and the §453 installment method that spreads gain over time. This week works each nonrecognition rule plus the loss-limitation traps (related parties, wash sales) and the special small-business stock benefits, all on the 2026 Public Law 119-21 baseline.

Section 1031 like-kind exchanges

A §1031 exchange defers gain when real property held for business or investment is exchanged for like-kind real property. Since the 2017 Act, §1031 applies to real property only — equipment and other personal property no longer qualify. Gain is deferred, not eliminated: it is preserved in a carryover basis in the replacement property. If the taxpayer receives boot (cash or non-like-kind property, including net debt relief), gain is recognized to the extent of the lesser of realized gain or boot received. Losses are never recognized in a like-kind exchange. Strict 45-day identification and 180-day completion deadlines apply to deferred exchanges.

Boot and basis mechanics

Worked example: MBG exchanges land (adjusted basis $200,000, fair value $300,000) for like-kind land worth $260,000 plus $40,000 cash. Realized gain is $100,000; recognized gain is the lesser of $100,000 or $40,000 boot = $40,000. The basis of the replacement land is the carryover basis $200,000 + $40,000 gain recognized − $40,000 boot received = $200,000, preserving the $60,000 of deferred gain. The basis formula — old basis plus gain recognized minus boot received plus boot paid — is the heart of every exchange problem.

Section 1033 involuntary conversions

When property is destroyed, stolen, or condemned and the taxpayer receives insurance or a condemnation award, §1033 allows gain deferral if the proceeds are reinvested in qualifying replacement property within the replacement period — generally two years after the year of gain (three years for condemned real property used in a business or held for investment). Gain is recognized only to the extent proceeds are not reinvested. Unlike §1031, §1033 is generally elective and the replacement need only be similar or related in service or use.

Section 121 home-sale exclusion

An individual may exclude up to $250,000 ($500,000 for married filing jointly) of gain on the sale of a principal residence, provided the ownership and use tests are met — owned and used as the principal residence for at least two of the five years before sale. The full exclusion is generally available once every two years; a partial exclusion is allowed for a sale forced by a change in employment, health, or unforeseen circumstances. Gain above the exclusion is capital gain, and any depreciation taken (for a home office) is recaptured as unrecaptured §1250 gain.

Installment sales

The installment method (§453) spreads gain over the years payments are received: each payment recognizes gain equal to the payment times the gross-profit percentage (gross profit ÷ contract price). It applies automatically to gains from a sale with at least one payment after the year of sale, but it is not available for inventory/dealer dispositions, for losses, or for the recapture portion (§1245/§1250 recapture is recognized in full in the year of sale regardless of payments). MBG financing a buyer's purchase of surplus land over several years would use this method to defer recognizing the gain.

Loss-limitation traps

Several rules disallow losses. Under §267, a loss on a sale to a related party (family, or a >50% owned entity) is disallowed — though the related buyer may later use the disallowed loss to offset gain on a subsequent sale. The wash-sale rule (§1091) disallows a loss on stock or securities if substantially identical securities are purchased within 30 days before or after the sale; the disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement securities. These provisions stop taxpayers from harvesting a loss while keeping the economic position.

Small-business stock benefits

Two provisions reward investing in small corporations. §1244 lets an individual treat a loss on qualifying small-business stock as an ordinary loss (up to $50,000, or $100,000 on a joint return) rather than a capital loss. §1202 excludes gain on qualified small business stock (QSBS) held long enough; under the 2026 Public Law 119-21 rules, QSBS issued after enactment qualifies for a tiered exclusion — 50% at a 3-year hold, 75% at 4 years, and 100% at 5 years — with the per-issuer cap raised to $15 million and the corporate gross-asset ceiling raised to $75 million. Together they soften the downside and reward the upside of funding a new business.

Exchange timing and related-party limits

Deferred ("Starker") exchanges run on a strict clock: the replacement property must be identified within 45 days and received within 180 days of transferring the relinquished property — missing either deadline makes the whole transaction taxable. A qualified intermediary holds the proceeds so the taxpayer never has constructive receipt of cash. Special related-party rules also apply: if a §1031 exchange is made with a related party, both must hold the exchanged properties for two years, or the deferral is retroactively lost. These mechanical guardrails are tested precisely because they are where real exchanges most often fail.

What "like-kind" really means

For real property, like-kind is interpreted broadly — improved land can be exchanged for unimproved land, an office building for a warehouse, a fee interest for a long-term leasehold — as long as both are U.S. real property held for business or investment. It is the nature of the interest, not its grade or quality, that matters. Property held for personal use or as inventory (MBG's spec homes) never qualifies, which is why the held-for-investment requirement is the first thing to test in any exchange problem.

CMA bridge

When MBG rolls one investment parcel into another or finances a land sale to a buyer, the §1031 and §453 rules decide how much gain is taxed now versus deferred — a cash-flow decision the CFO models directly. The tax deferral is real working capital, which is why the entity-structuring work from REG Unit 2 and the property rules here feed the same planning.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply §1031 (real property only; defer gain; recognize lesser of gain or boot; no loss; carryover basis + gain − boot).
  2. Apply §1033 (reinvest within 2 years / 3 for condemned realty) and §121 ($250k/$500k; 2-of-5-year ownership/use).
  3. Use the installment method (gross-profit % × payment), excluding dealer/inventory, losses, and recapture (recognized fully in year of sale).
  4. Disallow §267 related-party losses and §1091 wash-sale losses (add to replacement basis); apply §1244 ordinary loss and §1202 QSBS tiered exclusion.

Recap: §1031 defers real-property exchange gain (recognized only to the lesser of gain or boot, never a loss, with carryover basis); §1033 defers involuntary-conversion gain on timely reinvestment; §121 excludes $250k/$500k of home gain after a 2-of-5-year ownership/use test; the installment method spreads gain by the gross-profit percentage but not for dealers, losses, or recapture; and the §267 related-party and §1091 wash-sale rules disallow losses while §1244 (ordinary loss) and the 2026 §1202 QSBS tiered 50/75/100% exclusion reward small-business investment.

flashcards.back: REAL property held for business/investment only. Defer gain (carryover basis); recognize the LESSER of realized gain or boot received; losses never recognized. 45-day ID / 180-day completion.
Replacement basis = old adjusted basis + gain recognized + boot paid − boot received. Preserves the deferred gain.
Basis $200k land for $260k land + $40k cash: realized gain $100k, recognized = lesser of $100k or $40k boot = $40k; new basis $200k.
Defer gain if proceeds reinvested in similar property within 2 years (3 for condemned business/investment realty). Elective; gain recognized to extent not reinvested.
Exclude $250k single / $500k MFJ of gain; owned + used as principal residence 2 of last 5 years; generally once every 2 years (partial for hardship).
Gain per payment = payment × gross-profit % (gross profit ÷ contract price). NOT for dealer/inventory, losses, or recapture (recapture recognized fully in year of sale).

§267: related-party loss disallowed (buyer may offset later gain). §1091 wash sale: loss disallowed if substantially identical securities bought within 30 days before/after; add disallowed loss to replacement basis.

§1244: ordinary loss up to $50k ($100k MFJ) on qualifying small-business stock. §1202 QSBS (post-OBBBA): 50%/75%/100% gain exclusion at 3/4/5-year holds; $15M per-issuer cap; $75M gross-asset ceiling.

questions.q: After the 2017 Act, §1031 like-kind exchange treatment applies only to:
choices: Real property held for business or investment
questions.explain: §1031 is now limited to real property held for business or investment; personal property no longer qualifies.

questions.q: Land (basis $200,000) is exchanged for like-kind land worth $260,000 plus $40,000 cash; realized gain is $100,000. Recognized gain is:
questions.explain: Recognized gain is the lesser of realized gain ($100,000) or boot received ($40,000) = $40,000.

questions.q: The §121 exclusion on a principal residence for married filing jointly is up to:
questions.explain: MFJ may exclude up to $500,000 ($250,000 single) after the 2-of-5-year ownership/use test.

questions.q: The installment method may NOT be used for:
choices: Dealer/inventory sales, losses, or the recapture portion
questions.explain: Installment reporting is unavailable for dealer/inventory dispositions, losses, and depreciation recapture (recognized fully in the year of sale).

questions.q: A loss on a sale of stock is disallowed under the wash-sale rule if substantially identical securities are bought:
choices: Within 30 days before or after the sale
questions.explain: §1091 disallows the loss if substantially identical securities are purchased within 30 days before or after; the loss is added to the replacement basis.

questions.q: Under §1244, a loss on qualifying small-business stock for a joint return is treated as ordinary up to:
questions.explain: §1244 allows ordinary-loss treatment up to $50,000 ($100,000 MFJ); the rest is capital loss.

questions.q: Under the 2026 §1202 rules, QSBS held at least five years receives a gain exclusion of:
questions.explain: Post-OBBBA QSBS uses a tiered exclusion: 50% at 3 years, 75% at 4 years, and 100% at 5 years.
